connection: ScratchPad contains prior experiments and the student knows local methods. No TimeClock requirement currently needs ref, out, or in parameters. Add an isolated ScratchPad parameter-passing experiment without distorting a production repository API.
objectives: Compare ordinary parameters with out, ref, and in for both value-type and reference-type arguments.
Use out to report a success result and an additional parsed value.
Use ref to demonstrate deliberate caller-visible reassignment.
Use in to pass a value through a readonly reference, then explain why the production domain does not currently need that optimization.

visuals.title: out reports a second value on the way out
visuals.explanation: bool TryParseHours(string text, out decimal hours) returns whether parsing succeeded and assigns hours -- two pieces of information from one call.

visuals.title: The caller must handle both outcomes
visuals.explanation: if (TryParseHours(text, out var hours)) uses hours in the success branch. The method must assign its out parameter before every return.

visuals.title: ref lets a method change caller-visible storage
visuals.explanation: A ref int parameter can replace the value stored in the caller's variable, so the change remains visible after the method returns.

visuals.title: in passes a readonly reference
visuals.explanation: The method can read the caller's value but cannot reassign through the in parameter. Avoiding copies can matter for larger structs; this lab demonstrates the mechanism without claiming the TimeClock domain needs it.

preQuiz.prompt: What does TryParseHours(text, out var hours) communicate?
options: A Boolean success result and an additional parsed value
A guarantee that every string is a valid decimal
A request to mutate the input text
preQuiz.explanation: The bool reports success while the out parameter carries the parsed decimal.

preQuiz.prompt: What must a method do with every out parameter before it returns?
options: Assign it on every return path
Convert it into a reference type
preQuiz.explanation: C# enforces definite assignment for out parameters.

preQuiz.prompt: What restriction does in place on the method parameter?
options: The method can read it but cannot reassign through it
The caller cannot read the value afterward
The method must assign it before returning
preQuiz.explanation: in passes a readonly reference. It is often considered when copying a larger struct would matter.

concept.title: Ordinary parameters receive values
paragraphs: By default, every C# method receives a copy of the argument value. For a value type such as int, the number itself is copied. For a reference type such as Employee, the reference is copied, so caller and method still point to the same object.

Reassigning an ordinary parameter never replaces the caller's variable. A method receiving an Employee normally can mutate the shared Employee object, but assigning a different Employee to its local parameter does not replace the caller's reference.

rows: Caller and parameter have independent values
Both references can reach the same mutable object

concept.title: out returns an additional value
paragraphs: A Try-style method can return success as bool and place the found value in an out parameter.
out works with value types and reference types. This is useful when absence or failure is expected, but it should not be added to a production API unless callers genuinely need that shape.
concept.code:
static bool TryParseHours(string text, out decimal hours) =>
    decimal.TryParse(text, out hours);

concept.title: ref permits caller-visible reassignment
paragraphs: ref works with value types and reference types. It lets a method read and replace the value stored in the caller's variable. With ref int, the method can replace the caller's number; with ref Employee, it can make the caller's variable refer to a different Employee.

A normal Employee parameter already allows mutation of the shared Employee object. ref is needed only when replacing the caller's Employee reference itself is part of the contract. The caller must initialize the variable first, and both the declaration and call site use ref so that behavior remains visible.
Use ref only when changing the caller's variable is genuinely part of the method's contract.
concept.code: static void Increment(ref int value) => value++;

concept.title: in passes a readonly reference
paragraphs: in works with value types and reference types. It passes an existing value by reference while preventing the method from assigning a replacement through that parameter. The method can still read and display the value.

For a reference type, in makes the parameter reference readonly; it does not make the referenced object immutable. The method cannot replace the parameter with another object, but it can still mutate that object's publicly mutable members.

Avoiding a copy can help with larger structs. This ScratchPad example uses decimal only to make the syntax observable; the TimeClock production API has no measured need to use in for its small, ordinary values.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does TryParseHours return bool while also using out decimal hours?
options: The bool reports success while hours carries the parsed value
A decimal cannot be returned normally
postQuiz.explanation: This is the Try-pattern: one result reports success and the out parameter carries an additional result.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if TryParseHours had a return path that did not assign hours?
options: The code would not compile -- C# requires every out parameter to be definitely assigned before the method returns, on every path
hours would automatically become a successful parsed value
Nothing -- out parameters are optional to assign
postQuiz.explanation: Definite assignment of out parameters is enforced by the compiler, not just a convention -- this is exactly why callers can trust entry after a true return.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is out a better fit than ref for the parsedHours result?
options: ref would require the caller to initialize the variable first, while the parsing method determines the output completely
No, ref and out are interchangeable in every situation with no difference
No, ref only works with value types
postQuiz.explanation: ref requires a meaningful incoming variable value; out fits a method that produces the value on the way out.

reflections.question: After writing TryParseHours, when would you choose a bool-plus-out Try method instead of a nullable return?
reflections.answer: Choose a Try method when expected failure should be explicit as a Boolean result and the surrounding API follows that convention. A nullable return can be simpler when one optional value is all the caller needs. The better choice is the one that makes absence and caller handling clearest, not a universal syntax rule.

reflections.question: Can you think of a genuine (not contrived) use for ref anywhere in this codebase as it might grow?
reflections.answer: There is no strong ref use in the current domain because its important models are classes: ordinary reference passing already lets methods mutate the same object. A future performance-sensitive component working with large structs, arrays, or spans might use ref access to avoid copies or update storage directly, but that should follow a measured requirement rather than be added speculatively.

reflections.question: Why does 'this domain doesn't need in' feel like a legitimate lesson outcome rather than an incomplete one?
reflections.answer: in exists mainly to avoid copying larger value types while preventing reassignment through the parameter. This domain currently passes small values such as int and DateTime, so the extra modifier would add ceremony without solving a demonstrated problem. Understanding when not to use a specialized feature is part of using it correctly.

whatBreaks: Failing to assign an out parameter on every return path prevents compilation. Removing ref from either Increment's declaration or call breaks the explicit caller-visible reassignment contract. Assigning to an in parameter also fails to compile because that parameter is readonly inside the method.
summary: Ordinary parameters receive a copy of the argument value. out adds a compiler-enforced output, ref permits deliberate caller-visible reassignment, and in passes a readonly reference. ScratchPad demonstrates all four; production code should use the specialized modifiers only when their contracts solve a real problem.
